planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Consort was bred for resistance to white pine blister rust, which black currants can carry and spread to nearby white pines.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Consort is a Canadian-bred black currant developed specifically for resistance to white pine blister rust, a disease black currants can host and spread to nearby white pines, which historically got the crop restricted or banned in parts of North America. This resistance makes Consort a legal, low-risk choice for gardeners in areas where white pines grow nearby. Berries are the classic strong, aromatic black currant flavor, best used cooked into jam, syrup, and baked goods rather than eaten fresh, since raw black currants are quite tart and intense. Black currants fruit mainly on one-year-old wood, so prune out the oldest, least productive canes each dormant season and encourage a steady supply of vigorous young growth from the base.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Currant and Gooseberry Production

common_name: Ben Sarek Currant (Compact High-Yield Black Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Ben Sarek is a compact Scottish-bred black currant that fits small gardens and containers better than most currant cultivars.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Ben Sarek is a Scottish Crop Research Institute black currant bred for a naturally compact, dense habit that stays notably smaller than older black currant cultivars while still producing very heavy crops of large, richly flavored berries. Its compact size makes it one of the better black currant choices for small gardens and large containers, where a full-sized black currant bush would quickly outgrow the space. Berries are strongly aromatic and tart, best cooked into jam, syrup, cordial, and baked goods. Black currants fruit mainly on one-year-old wood, so remove the oldest canes each dormant season to keep the compact bush renewing itself with vigorous young growth.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Currant and Gooseberry Production

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Titania is a vigorous Swedish-bred black currant valued for heavy yields and good resistance to leaf spot and mildew.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Titania is a Swedish-bred black currant selected for strong vigor, heavy and consistent yields, and good resistance to leaf spot and powdery mildew compared with older black currant cultivars. The large, glossy berries carry the classic intense, aromatic black currant flavor, best used cooked into jam, syrup, cordial, and baked goods rather than eaten fresh. The upright, vigorous bush establishes quickly and bears well from a young age. Black currants fruit mainly on one-year-old wood, so remove the oldest, least productive canes each dormant season to encourage the strong young growth that will carry next year's crop, and net the bushes as fruit ripens, since birds are highly attracted to currants.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Currant and Gooseberry Production

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Crandall is a clove currant selection that tolerates heat and humidity far better than European black and red currants, making it a realistic currant choice for Gulf South gardens.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Crandall is a selection of the American clove currant, native to the central United States and far more tolerant of heat and humidity than the European black and red currants that generally struggle south of zone 7. In spring, the bush covers itself in small, bright yellow flowers with an intense clove fragrance that perfumes the whole garden and draws early pollinators, followed in summer by large, sweet-tart black currants excellent for fresh eating as well as jam and preserves. Because it genuinely performs in warm climates, Crandall is one of the few currants a Gulf South gardener can grow successfully without fighting the plant's preference for cool summers. The naturally spreading, suckering habit forms an attractive informal hedge over time; prune out the oldest canes periodically to keep the planting vigorous and productive.
sources: University of Missouri Extension — Native Fruit for the Home Garden
Oklahoma State University Extension — Currants for Oklahoma

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Downing is a nineteenth-century American heirloom gooseberry still widely grown for its reliable production and good mildew resistance.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Downing is a nineteenth-century American gooseberry, a Houghton seedling introduced in the 1850s and still one of the most widely planted heirloom gooseberries because of its reliable production, vigorous growth, and good resistance to powdery mildew compared with many European gooseberry cultivars. Berries are medium-sized, pale green, and tart, excellent for pies, preserves, and sauces, picked slightly underripe for cooking or left to fully ripen for a milder, sweeter fresh-eating berry. The self-fertile bush needs no separate pollinator and bears reliably from a young age. Prune out wood older than three years each dormant season to keep the thorny bush productive and open enough for easy harvest, and site with some afternoon shade in hot climates, since gooseberries generally prefer cooler growing conditions than the Deep South provides.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Currant and Gooseberry Production
